strengths: Provides a theoretically grounded approach (Theorem 1) connecting random Fourier feature embeddings of occupancy measures to true MMD distances, giving a principled justification for using these embeddings as behavior representations rather than relying on ad-hoc proxy objectives like state reconstruction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six continuous control environments against five diverse and relevant baselines (RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora, DvD-ES, SMERL), covering hand-crafted, learned, evolutionary, and RL-based diversity approaches.

Uses three complementary evaluation metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, quality-weighted Vendi Score) to mitigate bias toward any single notion of diversity, which is a thoughtful methodological choice given the inherent difficulty of comparing methods with different diversity objectives.

Includes an additional application study (robustness to changed friction/mass dynamics) that demonstrates a practically meaningful benefit of the discovered diverse policy populations, going beyond simple benchmark scores.
Provides ablations on embedding dimension and behavioral descriptor dimension that offer useful insight into the trade-offs of the proposed cwPCA-based descriptor extraction.
Reasonably transparent reporting of failure cases (HalfCheetah, Walker2d) rather than only favorable results, and a candid limitations section.
Detailed appendices with algorithm pseudocode, proof, and hyperparameters that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 1) is derived for the embedding φ^π obtained via i.i.d. geometric-discount sampling, but the paper explicitly switches to a different, more data-efficient embedding ψ^π (Eq. 6) for practical use, without providing a matching theoretical analysis; the link between the proven guarantee and what is actually deployed is only informally motivated (same expectation), leaving a gap between theory and practice.

The dimensionality reduction step (cwPCA) that turns the theoretically-grounded high-dimensional embeddings into low-dimensional behavioral descriptors has no theoretical backing — it is a heuristic combination of fitness-weighted PCA and quantile calibration, so the paper's core practical algorithm is only partially supported by its theoretical contribution.

Only three random seeds are used per environment/method, which is relatively limited for QD-RL and evolutionary strategy experiments known to have high variance; conclusions in close cases (e.g., qVS/VS differences between AutoQD and RegularQD in Walker2d) may not be fully reliable at this sample size.

No comparison to more recent/stronger gradient-based QD methods (e.g., PPGA, DQD, PGA-MAP-Elites) that are cited as state-of-the-art in the related work, despite being readily combinable with the proposed descriptor discovery method; this leaves open whether AutoQD's gains persist with stronger underlying optimizers.

No reporting of computational overhead/wall-clock comparisons between AutoQD and baselines, despite AutoQD requiring periodic RFF-based embedding computation and cwPCA updates, which is relevant for practical adoption alongside Aurora/LSTM-Aurora's autoencoder retraining costs.

The case studies in HalfCheetah and Walker2d suggest that PCA-derived directions of maximal fitness-weighted variance do not necessarily correspond to behaviorally meaningful or interpretable diversity (e.g., 'sliding' policies, over-emphasis on foot joints), suggesting the descriptor discovery may still miss interesting diversity dimensions much like hand-crafted BDs, undercutting part of the motivating claim that automatic descriptors avoid this pitfall.

The kernel bandwidth for the RFF embedding is fixed via a simple heuristic and not ablated or adaptively tuned, which the authors themselves note as a limitation but do not empirically explore, leaving the sensitivity of results to this choice unclear.

strengths: Presents a theoretically grounded approach to automatic behavior descriptor discovery, exploiting the well-known policy-occupancy-measure correspondence combined with random Fourier feature approximations of MMD; this gives a principled alternative to heuristic autoencoder-based unsupervised BD methods (Aurora, LSTM-Aurora).

Rigorous theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 with a full, careful proof (including an extension in Appendix B justifying the practical trajectory-averaged embedding used in the algorithm, and even acknowledging finite-horizon truncation bias), giving concrete, non-asymptotic finite-sample/finite-dimension convergence guarantees connecting embedding distances to true MMD between occupancy measures.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six standard continuous-control benchmarks against five diverse and relevant baselines (RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora, DvD-ES, SMERL), using multiple complementary QD/diversity metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, quality-weighted Vendi Score), with AutoQD outperforming baselines in most settings.

Extensive and honest ancillary analyses: quality-diversity trade-off scatter plot, fine-grained per-task statistics, adaptation-to-dynamics-shift experiments (friction/mass), ablations on embedding dimension, BD dimension, weighting mechanism, and number of rollouts for descriptor stability, plus qualitative visualization of discovered behaviors -- this thoroughness is a notable strength for reproducibility and understanding of the method's behavior.

Clear, well-motivated method exposition (Fig. 1/2, Algorithm 1) and reasonably complete implementation/hyperparameter details in the appendix; the paper explicitly discusses failure cases (HalfCheetah, Walker2d) and offers plausible explanations rather than hiding weaknesses.

The cwPCA weighting scheme and calibration procedure are practically motivated and empirically ablated, showing the authors considered subtle interactions between the QD algorithm and the learned descriptor space.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 1) is an asymptotic/high-probability bound that requires the trajectory-embeddings to come from i.i.d. samples of the true occupancy measure; the practical implementation (single evaluation batch of n=5 rollouts, fixed kernel bandwidth, fixed random features reused across the entire run in Algorithm 1) may not tightly satisfy the theorem's assumptions, and the paper does not empirically validate how well the theoretical convergence rate is realized in practice (e.g., no plot of embedding-distance vs. ground truth MMD error as n or D scale).

Only 3 random seeds are used for main experiments (Table 1), which is a relatively small sample size for stochastic RL/QD experiments and makes some of the close comparisons (e.g., AutoQD vs. RegularQD in Walker2d, or vs. Aurora in HalfCheetah) statistically weak; no significance tests are reported for the main results table (unlike the cwPCA ablation, which does use Mann-Whitney U).

AutoQD introduces a nontrivial set of extra hyperparameters (embedding dimension D, kernel bandwidth, discount factor for the embedding, descriptor dimension k, update schedule for cwPCA) that are fixed to specific values across all six environments without a systematic sensitivity/robustness study beyond BipedalWalker; it's unclear how transferable these choices are to substantially different domains (e.g., higher-dimensional or image-based observations, acknowledged as future work).

Combining AutoQD with the current SOTA gradient-based QD algorithms (PGA-ME/PPGA) is stated to be 'non-trivial' and left as future work, while PGA-ME with ground-truth descriptors clearly outperforms CMA-MAE-based methods on several metrics (Table 8); this leaves open the question of how competitive AutoQD would be against a truly SOTA QD-RL pipeline rather than only CMA-MAE variants, somewhat limiting the significance of the reported improvements.

The identified failure modes (premature convergence to simple/stable behaviors such as HalfCheetah sliding or Walker2d bottom-joint-only gaits) suggest a fundamental limitation of the low-dimensional occupancy-measure projection approach that is not fully resolved, only mitigated by hand-tuning descriptor dimensionality; the paper acknowledges but does not solve this core exploration issue.

The comparison baselines for skill-discovery/unsupervised RL literature is limited to only SMERL (justified by code availability), omitting DIAYN, DADS, or DoMiNo, which somewhat narrows the empirical positioning of AutoQD relative to the broader unsupervised RL literature discussed in Related Work.

The evaluation metrics themselves (VS, qVS) rely on RFF-based kernel embeddings structurally very similar to those AutoQD itself uses to define its behavior space, which, despite the authors' claim of a 'larger, separate' set of features for fairness, introduces a degree of metric-method alignment that could inflate AutoQD's apparent advantage on diversity metrics compared to methods whose behavior spaces are defined very differently (e.g., hand-crafted RegularQD descriptors).
